title: The Enduring Impact of the American Dust Bowl: Short and Long-run Adjustments to Environmental Catastrophe
research_question: How large and persistent are the agricultural and economic costs of severe, permanent soil erosion on the American Plains during the 1930s? To what extent do affected areas adjust over the short and long run through reallocation of farmland across uses, changes in capital and labor inputs, migration, and expansion of non-agricultural sectors, and how much of the initial agricultural cost is recovered through these adjustments?
data_description: The analysis uses a balanced panel of 769 Plains counties (held to 1910 borders) covering 12 Plains states from 1910 through the 1990s, drawn primarily from decennial and quinquennial U.S. Census of Agriculture and Population data (Gutmann 2005; Haines 2005). County-level variables include per-acre farmland values, agricultural revenues, capital/equipment, cropland and pasture acreage, crop-specific output and acreage (wheat, hay, corn, cotton, oats), livestock counts, number and average size of farms, fallow land, total and rural and farm population, retail sales per capita, unemployment, and manufacturing employment, payroll, establishments, and value added. Supplementary data include county-level erosion classifications (low/medium/high topsoil loss) digitized from a Soil Conservation Service map at the National Archives, FDIC banking records (1920-1936), New Deal expenditure data (Fishback et al. 2005), and Palmer Drought Severity Index and temperature data from the National Climatic Data Center.
institutional_context: During the 1930s the American Plains experienced an unprecedented environmental catastrophe combining severe drought with intensive plow-based cultivation of native grasslands that had expanded after World War I. Massive wind storms stripped topsoil and heavy rains carved gullies, leaving some areas with cumulative losses exceeding 75% of original topsoil by 1940, while neighboring areas were largely spared. This produced sharp local variation in permanent land productivity within the same states. The shock coincided with the Great Depression, restricted credit access, and bank failures, and prompted federal responses including the 1933 Agricultural Adjustment Act, the establishment of the Soil Conservation Service, the 1935-1936 Soil Conservation and Domestic Allotment Acts, and later the Conservation Reserve Program. The setting offers spatial heterogeneity in a large, persistent productivity shock to a fixed factor (land), enabling examination of agricultural reallocation, migration, wages, and industrial development over decades.
